title: Breed Rankings
text:
The Breed Rank data gives information about different types of breek ranks. The specific dataset called breed_rank_all gives information about the ranking of each dog breed recorded from the years 2013 to 2020. There are 195 different types of breeds that this data set contains.
This data set is a Breed Rankings Dataset from Kkakey courtesy of American Kennel Club. This data has been made available by KKakey through the TidyTuesday Data Link

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

breed_rank_all <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2022/2022-02-01/breed_rank.csv')


ggplot(breed_rank_all, aes(x = `2013 Rank`, y = `2020 Rank`)) + 
    geom_point() +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
    labs(title = "Dog Breed Rankings 2013 vs 2020" )








The graph compares the dog breed rankings from the year 2013 to the year 2020. The red slope line attemps to highlight how the ranking between each year doesn’t change much. It would be interesting to learn more about which specific breeds are farther away from this trendline.

title: Simpson Episodes
text:
This data set analyzes the episodes from the TV show The Simpsons. Episodes and script lines have been filtered to only include episodes from 2010 to 2016. The data contains information about the imdb rating, voting, number in the series, season, title, views, and more.
This dataset is a Simpsons Dataset from Kaggle which was made available to the public by Prashant Banerjee. Thank you to Nicolas Foss, Ed.D., MS with Iowa HHS who curated the data set in linked in TidyTuesday

library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

simpsons_episodes <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-02-04/simpsons_episodes.csv')


ggplot(simpsons_episodes, aes(x = views, y = imdb_rating)) + 
    geom_point() +
    labs(title = "Rating vs Views of Simpsons Episodes" )








The graph compares the imdb rating to the views of each Simpson episode within the data set. While most of the data points are skewed to the right side, there are a handful of episodes that have 0 or close to 0 views, yet relatively good ratings. Overall, the greater the number of views, the greater the rating is.

title: The Office Quotes
text:
This data set has information on all of the lines spoken in the American sitcom show, The Office. The data set tracks all lines from all 9 seasons and includes the season, episode, line, character who spoke the line, and what number line it was in the entire show. In total there are 61,306 lines!
This dataset has been created by Kaggle and was originally scraped from a website called Office Quotes that is currently down.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

office_lines <- read.csv("the-office_lines.csv")



The code below gives you a ranking of each character, calculating the length of lines for each character from The Office. I calculated the length of each line for each character and the summed up the length of all of their lines.



Code
office_lines_changed <- office_lines |>
  group_by(Character) |>
  mutate(line_length = str_length(Line))|>
  summarize(total_length = sum(line_length, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(total_length)) |>
  head(10)




One of the most common phrases that is repeated in The Office is “That’s what she said.” The main character Michael often repeats this innapropriate joke and I wanted to count how many times this joke was repeated by each character. First I found it helpful to change each string to all lower case and then use a regular expression brackets to choose either a straight or curly apostrophe.



Code
office_lines |>
  mutate(Line = str_to_lower(Line))|>
  group_by(Character) |>
  summarize(exclaim_counter = sum(str_count(Line, "that['’]s what she said")))|>
  arrange(desc(exclaim_counter))

PLOT 1: Length of Lines of Characters in The Office If you wanted to see how big of a role each character has in The Office throughout all 9 seasons, one way to track this could be to calculate the length of their lines. From this plot we can see that Michael, the main character, speaks the most. I was surprised to see that Andy spoke more than Pam because I always thought Pam was one of the more prevelant characters in the show. Using concept of tracking the times Dwight is mentioned in the Office, I plotted how many times Dwight is mentioned in each season. This gives us insight to how often the other characters talk about Dwight each season. With this data we can see that generally over time his popularity in the show increases. Although in season 2 and 3 Dwight is mentioned a lot more than in Season 4, 6, and 7. It would be interested to compare the data of all of the other characters and see which seasons highlight individual plots for each character. Maybe Dwight is mentioned less in Season 4 because Jim and Pam start dating then and are mentioned more by other characters.

title: Air Quality
text:
The UK Weather data set explores climate data such as mean daily minimum and maximum temperatures, total rainfall, total sunshine hours and days of frost for each month in each year starting from 1941. The Historic UK Meteorological & Climate Data has been provided by the UK Met Office which is the national weather service in the UK. Thank you to Jack Davison who scraped the data and published it to Tidy Tuesday


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

UK_weather <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-10-21/historic_station_met.csv')


In the UK, the summers are often warm, however within the past few years there have been record high temperatures during the month of July. I thought it would be interesting to uncover the data from the month of July from an earlier range of years to a later range.

title: UK Weather
text:
The UK Weather data set explores climate data such as mean daily minimum and maximum temperatures, total rainfall, total sunshine hours and days of frost for each month in each year from 1930s to 2024. The Historic UK Meteorological & Climate Data has been provided by the UK Met Office which is the national weather service in the UK. Thank you to Jack Davison who scraped the data and published it to Tidy Tuesday


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)

uk_weather <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-10-21/historic_station_met.csv')


In the UK, the weather is varied: some months bring very high temperatures, while others are cold. July is known to be one of the months whose weather has changed the most over the years. Using weather data from the 1940s to the 2020s from several weather stations around the UK, I hope to compare rainfall with maximum temperature in July of each year. Rain can occur at both low and high temperatures, how can we begin to understand this relationship?
My research question: Is there a correlation between maximum temperature and total rainfall in July?
To understand this question, I have chosen to focus on two stations: Heathrow and Lerwick. Heathrow is a station that is not far from central London, whereas Lerwick is the most northern station in the UK. I thought it would be interesting to compare the data of these two stations.

title: UK Weather
text:
Station Heathrow

Welcome to Heathrow!
If you are traveling to London, England you might land in London Heathrow Airport. It is one of the world’s busiest aviation hubs. Fun Fact! Did you know that there is in fact a secret terminal called The Windsor where only royal family members, diplomats, and VIP flyers can take off from?
From the data in the UK weather dataset, here is the scatterplot that helps us understand how rainfall and maximum temperature in the month of July are possibly related.


Code
heathrow_july <- uk_weather |>
  filter(station == "heathrow", month == 7) |>
  select(station, month, year, tmax, rain) 

ggplot(heathrow_july, aes(x = tmax, y = rain))+
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Heathrow Rainfall vs Max Temperature in July 1948-2024",
    x = "Maximum Temperature (°C)", 
    y = "Rainfall (mm)", 
    caption = "Figure 1"
    ) +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)) 









Figure 1 illustrates the relationship between maximum temperature in July and rainfall at the Heathrow Station. The general trend shows that as the maximum temperature increases, the rainfall decreases.


Code
correlation_heathrow <- heathrow_july |>
  summarize(r = cor(tmax, rain)) |>
  pull(r)
cat("The calculated correlation between rainfall and maximum temperature at Heathrow station is: ", correlation_heathrow)


The calculated correlation between rainfall and maximum temperature at Heathrow station is:  -0.482847

text:
Applying Shuffling to Heathrow Data


Code
set.seed(47)
shuffle_plot <- shuffle_points(1, heathrow_july)

ggplot(shuffle_plot, aes(x = shuffle_temp, y = rain)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Heathrow Rainfall vs. Shuffled Max \n Temperature",
    x = "Shuffled Max Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Rainfall (mm)"
  )











Code
set.seed(47)
shuffled_heathrow <- map(1:1000, shuffle_correlation, dataframe = heathrow_july)|>
list_rbind()

shuffled_heathrow |>
  ggplot(aes(x = correlation)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = correlation_heathrow, color = "red", linewidth = 1)+
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = correlation_heathrow,
    y = Inf,
    label = paste("observed r =", round(correlation_heathrow, 3)),
    color = "red",
    hjust = -0.05,
    vjust = 1.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation of Shuffled Temperature \n vs Rainfall at Heathrow", 
    x = "Temperature and Rainfall Correlation",
    y = "Number of Shuffles"
  )

title: UK Weather
text:
Lerwick Station
While Heathrow Station resides just outside of central London, Lerwick is the most northern meteorological station in the UK. As a result, I wondered if the correlation between maximum temperature and rainfall in July would be any different.


Code
lerwick_july <- uk_weather |>
  filter(station == "lerwick", month == 7) |>
  select(station, month, year, tmax, rain)

ggplot(lerwick_july, aes(x = tmax, y = rain))+
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Lerwick Rainfall vs Max Temperature in July 1931-2024", 
    x = "Maximum Temperature (°C)", 
    y = "Rainfall (mm)", 
    caption = "Figure 4"
    )+ 
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)) 









Figure 4 above shows a plot of the maximum temperatures during July vs the rainfall measured at Lerwick Station. In comparison to Figure 1 (Heathrow Station), the dots are more scattered and don’t follow a general trend.


Code
correlation_lerwick <- lerwick_july |>
  summarize(r = cor(tmax, rain)) |>
  pull(r)
cat("The calculated correlation between rainfall and maximum temperature at Lerwick station is: ", correlation_lerwick)


The calculated correlation between rainfall and maximum temperature at Lerwick station is:  -0.05910021

section: Applying Hypothesis Testing to Heathrow Data
text:
Applying Hypothesis Testing to Heathrow Data


Code
set.seed(47)
shuffle_plot_heathrow <- shuffle_points(1, heathrow_july)

ggplot(shuffle_plot_heathrow, aes(x = shuffle_temp, y = rain)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Heathrow Rainfall vs. Shuffled Max Temperature",
    x = "Shuffled Max Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Rainfall (mm)", 
    caption = "Figure 2"
  ) +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)) 









Figure 2 represents the shuffled maximum temperatures vs the rainfall when the temperatures are shuffled once. In simple terms, this means that the assigned maximum temperatures have been shuffled randomly. In the graph above we can see that the shuffled temperatures don’t have a similar negative correlation as the original graph. To understand more we need to map the shuffle function multiple times. By mapping we are iterating this shuffling correlation function a thousand times which will give us lots of data points.


Code
set.seed(47)
shuffled_heathrow <- map(1:1000, shuffle_correlation, dataframe = heathrow_july)|>
list_rbind()   

shuffled_heathrow |>
  ggplot(aes(x = correlation)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = correlation_heathrow, color = "red", linewidth = 1)+
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = correlation_heathrow,
    y = Inf,
    label = paste("observed r =", round(correlation_heathrow, 3)),
    color = "red",
    hjust = -0.05,
    vjust = 1.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation of Shuffled Temperature vs Rainfall at Heathrow", 
    x = "Temperature and Rainfall Correlation",
    y = "Number of Shuffles", 
    caption = "Figure 3"
  ) +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)) 









Figure 3 represents the mapped correlation values for rainfall and maximum temperature in July at Heathrow Station. The mapping line of code applies the shuffle_correlation function a thousand times which shuffles the temperatures a thousand times and then spits out 1 correlation value for each shuffle. As we can see, the red line to the left of the histogram is far from the correlation values. The red line represents the original observed correlation value which was calculated to be -0.483. Since the correlation is far from the correlation calculated by the random shuffling temperature, we can make the conclusion that there is a negative correlation: As maximum temperature increases in July, the rainfall decreases.

P-Value


Code
shuffled_heathrow |>
  summarize(p_value = mean(abs(correlation) >= abs(correlation_heathrow)))


# A tibble: 1 × 1
  p_value
    <dbl>
1       0


The p-value calculated above supports the previous statement that we reject the null hypothesis. Therefore the observed data did not happen just by chance or randomness.

title: UK Weather
text:
Applying Shuffling to Lerwick Data
Again, to begin our investigation of the correlation between rainfall and maximum temperature we need to test the null hypothesis. The null hypothesis is the test that there is no relationship between these two variables. We are testing if the values of rainfall and maximum temperature happen just by random chance.


Code
set.seed(123)
shuffle_plot_lerwick <- shuffle_points(1, lerwick_july)

ggplot(shuffle_plot_lerwick, aes(x = shuffle_temp, y = rain)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Lerwick Rainfall vs. Shuffled Max Temperature",
    x = "Shuffled Max Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Rainfall (mm)", 
    caption = "Figure 5"
  ) +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)) 









Similar to Figure 2, Figure 5 illustrates the shuffled maximum temperatures vs rainfall in Lerwick Station when the temperatures were shuffled once. However, to investigate the null hypothesis we map the shuffle function of the lerwick data multiple times.


Code
set.seed(47)
shuffled_lerwick <- map(1:1000, shuffle_correlation, dataframe = lerwick_july)|>
list_rbind()

shuffled_lerwick |>
  ggplot(aes(x = correlation)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = correlation_lerwick, color = "red", linewidth = 1)+
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = correlation_lerwick,
    y = Inf,
    label = paste("observed r =", round(correlation_lerwick, 3)),
    color = "red",
    hjust = -0.05,
    vjust = 1.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation of Shuffled Temperature vs Rainfall at Lerwick", 
    x = "Temperature and Rainfall Correlation",
    y = "Number of Shuffles", 
    caption = "Figure 6"
  )+
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)) 









While the process of mapping and iterating the shuffle function was similar to the Heathrow Data, Figure 6 illustrates how the relationship between temperature and rainfall was different in the two stations. The red correlation value which is -0.059 overlaps with correlation of shuffled temperatures vs rainfall. Unlike Figure 3, we are unable to make the conclusion that there is a distinct relationship between rainfall and maximum temperature because the correlation falls in the region where randomness could have occurred. Not only does it fall in the region, but it is less than 0.1 off of the most central and peak part of the graph. Since the correlation values falls in this region, we need more information/cannot make a conclusion that these two variables depend on each other directly.

P-Value


Code
shuffled_lerwick |>
  summarize(p_value = mean(abs(correlation) >= abs(correlation_lerwick)))


# A tibble: 1 × 1
  p_value
    <dbl>
1   0.548


According to statistics, if the p value is greater than a value of 0.05, then that data fails to reject the null hypothesis. In this scenario the value of the p value calculated above is 0.548 which is a lot greater than 0.05, and there we cannot reject the idea of randomness.

title: ShotSpotter Surveillance on Black and Brown Communities
text:
Introduction to Ethical Dilemma
ShotSpotter is an acoustic gunshot detection technology that identifies the sound of the gunshot, location, and alerts law enforcement agencies. ShotSpotter outlined its Community Privacy Protections emphasizing that the risk for voice surveillance is extremely low.
Prior to activating the sensors, ShotSpotter works with their clients to determine the location they want to be covered by ShotSpotter, targeting the areas with most gun violence. When the coverage is set, engineers determine exact location of the sensors, police do not have a say in the placement. ShotSpotter sensors are only triggered by an instantaneous, sharp noise and therefore cannot hear human voices. When a noise is detected the audio is sent to a ShotSpotter employee and they confirm whether the sound could be a gunshot. After determining gunfire, police are notified and provided with the recording and location. After the incident recordings are deleted after 30 hours and are only accessible under strict conditions if a gunshot is missed. According to their privacy protections, ShotSpotter is here to provide surveillance that will have social benefits of decrease in gun violence.
In March 2024, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) reported that ShotSpotter technology was being implemented in communities of color significantly more than other communities. Internal documents were leaked to WIRED which exposed the locations of ShotSpotter’s nationwide network of microphones. The ACLU highlights that along with many other cities, in Milwaukee the technology was placed in North and South sides of the city which are majority Latinx and Black communities.
In their article, ACLU referenced studies that illustrated how ShotSpotter was highly ineffective as 89% of the gunshot alerts did not lead to police force finding gun-related incidents. Additionally, sensors were triggered by other loud sounds such as fireworks or car back-firing.
The ACLU argues that the use of ShotSpotter in police force is not only highly ineffective but could lead to dangerous situations especially for Black and Brown communities as they are targeted for surveillance. Instead of investing in inaccurate surveillance technology, they urge police force to invest in public safety solutions that address ongoing issues.
In another article written by ACLU, Jay Stanley illustrates how increased surveillance in communities of color has led to more frequent searches. As a result, by targeting communities of color there is an increased risk of further violence against communities of color.
There are many parts to the ethical dilemma. One part is whether it is ethical to survey citizens without their consent. The second part of the dilemma is whether or not it is worth investing money into a technology that is mean to protect communities when the outcome is instead targeting and endangering those communities further. The most important part of the dilemma in my opinion is if it ethical to survey a specific community that has been increasingly targeted due to racial systematic bias in the United States and across the world. Additionally it is important to consider that increased surveillance has also lead to increased number of deaths against people of color, and increase number of moments of police brutality.


Understanding the Ethical Considerations

1. What was the consent structure for recruiting participants? Were the participants aware of the ways their data would be used for research? Was informed consent possible? Can you provide informed consent for applications that are yet foreseen?
The Wisconsin Examiner investigated the leaked data on ShotSpotter and highlighted how contracts were disclosed and there was a significant increase in money spent on ShotSpotter by the City of Milwaukee from 2010 to 2023. However, some of the contract money was offset by state funding which makes it harder to understand how much money the city spent on ShotSpotter in 2023. While general contracts were disclosed, people were not able to know the specific locations of the ShotSpotter sensors or the audio recording capabilities. As a result, one could argue that the surveillance was a violation of people’s privacy. Although in ShotSpotter’s privacy protections it states that audio recording is only triggered by a loud instantaneous noise, they did not disclose if human noise could be heard after or during the recording. If people were unaware that their voices could be heard, they did not consent to surveillance.
Police force have disclosed incidents and given information to the timestamp which can be found in the Justice Tech Lab archives, however the location has been redacted. I imagine that location has been kept secret so that audio sensors are not vandalized and so that police can catch more recordings of gunshots because people do not know they are nearby a sensor. The Wisconsin Examiner supported the theory as they summarized how the department refused to give information on the locations of the sensors because it would hinder the police force’s ability to respond to crime and endanger citizens who have agreed to have sensors on their property.


2. How were the variables collected? Were they accurately recorded? Is there any missing data?
The variables were collected by ShotSpotter sensors and then sent to the police force. According to ACLU, what was intended to be recorded, gunshots, were in fact not accurately recorded. Most of the data collected were false positives. In other words, the ShotSpotter sensors mistook other loud noises for gunshots and sent police into those locations where no evidence of crime was found.
Since the ShotSpotter privacy policy has emphasized that their sensors only rely on audio, there is a significant amount of missing data for each report. There is no information on what object has made the sound, how many people were around during the time of the sound and the weather both I imagine could have triggered the sensors in extreme situations give ShotSpotter’s description of how audio recordings turn on. There is also missing data on how the ShotSpotter classifies what is a gunshot and what is not. The ShotSpotter privacy protections have written that if a loud noise triggers the recording algorithm that an employee will listen and confirm whether or not the sound is similar to a gunshot. There is missing data on who confirmed the sound and what the sound was like. Since the sensors are a surveillance tool used by police, there are many parts of missing data that the general public is not able to view.


3. Who was measured? Are those individuals representative of the people to whom we’d like to generalize / apply the algorithm? Should we analyze data if we do not know how the data were collected?
What was measured was the sound of the alleged gunshot and the location of the sensor. As the ACLU and the Wisconsin Examiner illustrated, the sensors in Milwaukee were more frequently placed in Black and Brown communities. These individuals in the communities with sensors were overrepresented in the data. According to ShotSpotter’s privacy protections, the sensors were placed in locations with the gun violence. However, when the locations were leaked, news reporters such as the ACLU and Wisconsin Examiner noticed sensors were not evenly distributed. Therefore, there is missing data on communities that were not targeted.
The data is still worth analyzing because it tells us how ineffective the sensors were as they displayed false positives a majority of the time. Additionally, the data that the public got as a result of the data leak was able to tell us about the specific locations of the sensors. I think the ShotSpotter data is especially helpful to analyze in deciding whether targeted surveillance is ethically okay. The data on the locations of the sensors led to discussions where people advocated for knowing more about how data is being collection. Therefore, analyzing data might give you an answer that you might not have predicted, but could bring up important discussions and questions.


4. Is the data being used in unintended ways to the original study?
In another article by ACLU titled, “Four Problems with the ShotSpotter Gunshot Detection System”, Jay Stanley highlighted how the increased ShotSpotter incidents reported to the police has led to an increase in stop and frisk searches in the communities with sensors. The original point of the data was to investigate whether a gunshot incident had occurred in a specific location. However, does the audio recording give enough evidence for police to stop and search people in the area around the sensors. The main goal of ShotSpotter that was outlined in the privacy protections was to decrease the number of gun related incidents using the audio recordings, however, they never specified that using those recordings would increase the stops and searches in those neighborhoods. Stanley also argued that increased surveillance can distort gun statistics and create justification for surveying communities of color more, creating a cycle of injustice.



Conclusion
The ShotSpotter ethical dilemma has many affects to both the communities of color and to our society as a whole. The problem that stems from the ethical dilemma is that people of color in the United States and across the world are targeted and surveyed much more than white communities. The audio surveillance created by ShotSpotter opens up opportunity for increased manual surveillance (pat downs and searches) by police force. While both ShotSpotter and police systems pitch the surveillance system as a way to reduce gun violence, there are many flaws in the system. For example, ShotSpotter cannot detect gunshot sounds easily and often mistake other sounds as a gunshot, leading to increased police patrol and surveillance in communities of color (where the audio sensors are placed). Therefore, the police force is able to control these communities at the expense of their safety in their own homes. Like many other ethical dilemmas in our world now, the ShotSpotter surveillance dilemma is about power, who controls the right to survey certain communities and how one can justify surveying those communities. In our world right now, it is especially important to question whether or not things are right and who is harmed. Oftentimes, we as a society fail to recognize who is negatively harmed by decisions of large companies and people in power.
